A C++ compiler flag that is described as affecting “only” preprocessor macro conformance can still change the compilation of CUDA translation units because the preprocessor is not a cosmetic front end: it determines the exact token stream that the compiler sees. In an MSVC/CUDA build, `nvcc` invokes the host compiler and host preprocessor for the host portion of the translation unit, and CUDA source files routinely include CCCL headers such as Thrust, CUB, and libcudacxx. Those headers contain large amounts of conditional compilation and macro-based feature detection, for example around `__CUDACC__`, `__CUDA_ARCH__`, CUDA compiler version macros, MSVC version macros, C++ standard macros, and internal CCCL macros that select code paths, enable or disable overloads, choose implementation details, or work around compiler defects.

`/Zc:preprocessor` changes MSVC’s preprocessor behavior toward a more conforming model. That can alter the expansion of variadic macros, the handling of empty macro arguments, `__VA_OPT__`, token pasting, stringification, macro recursion, and other macro-expansion corner cases. If a CCCL header contains a macro whose expansion depends on those rules, then enabling `/Zc:preprocessor` can cause a different sequence of tokens to be produced after preprocessing. Those different tokens can cause different `#if`/`#ifdef` branches to be taken, different template instantiations to be generated, different inline functions or specializations to be selected, or different CUDA/host code paths to be compiled. Thus, even though the flag is nominally a preprocessor-conformance flag, it can change the semantic input to the compiler and therefore change the generated host or device code.

A bitwise-identical greedy decoding comparison between two builds proves only that the observable numerical outputs are identical for the tested inputs and execution conditions. Greedy decoding is deterministic if the same model, input, kernel selection, reduction order, floating-point operations, and execution environment are used. If the decoded token sequences and associated logits or probabilities are bitwise identical, that is strong evidence that the executed code paths produced the same floating-point results for that workload. It can rule out observable differences caused by changed kernel selection, changed template instantiation, changed vectorization, changed floating-point contraction, changed reduction order, or changed arithmetic semantics, at least for the tested cases.

However, bitwise-identical greedy decoding does not prove that the two builds generated identical machine code, identical PTX/SASS, identical object files, or identical template instantiations. It also does not prove that `/Zc:preprocessor` had no effect on compilation. It only proves functional equivalence of the observed outputs under the tested conditions. Different generated code can produce identical results, and code differences may exist in paths that were not exercised by the comparison. To prove that the generated code is identical, one would need to compare the relevant artifacts directly, such as object files, PTX, SASS, disassembly, or compiler-generated intermediate representations.

In short, `/Zc:preprocessor` can change CUDA/CCCL compilation because macro conformance changes the token stream and therefore the conditional code that is compiled, while bitwise-identical greedy decoding proves only output equivalence for the tested workload, not identity of the generated code.
